abstract: Host-associated microbiomes are increasingly recognized as important components of cnidarian biology, yet their diversity and organization remain poorly understood in non-coral lineages, particularly in polar environments. Staurozoans, or stalked jellyfishes, are a small and understudied group of benthic medusozoans whose associated bacterial communities remain largely unexplored. Here, we used 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing to characterize bacterial communities associated with the Antarctic stalked jellyfish Haliclystus antarcticus collected from two coastal sites in the South Shetland Islands, Byers Bay and Risopatron. We examined three anatomical compartments (gut, peduncle, and tentacles) to investigate patterns of bacterial community diversity and composition. Gut samples exhibited the greatest variability in richness-based alpha diversity, whereas peduncle and tentacle samples displayed more constrained diversity profiles. Across compartments, 47 amplicon sequence variants (ASVs) were shared, indicating a recurrent bacterial component within the host-associated communities. Gut samples exhibited the strongest differential-abundance signal, while genera such as Polaribacter and Planktotalea were identified as indicators of tentacle-associated communities. In parallel, we isolated and characterized a gut-associated bacterium identified as Oceanisphaera ostreae. Genomic and metabolomic analyses revealed diverse biosynthetic potential and multiple metabolite-related features. Preliminary bioactivity screening indicated antibacterial activity against Staphylococcus aureus, with no cytotoxicity detected against HCT-116 cells under the tested conditions. Together, these results provide the first characterization of the H. antarcticus microbiome, demonstrating anatomical and geographic variation in bacterial communities and identifying a cultivable bacterial associate with potentially relevant metabolic capabilities.
